prompt.context: Your client, SaveMart, is a discount superstore similar to Wal-Mart. They have 1,000 retail stores across the United States. Each store receives one delivery per day from a distribution center. SaveMart has hired you to investigate if the costs related to distribution can be reduced. SaveMart owns multiple distribution centers across the United States. The 4 primary distribution centers are located in New York, Chicago, Dallas, and San Francisco. The 20 secondary distribution centers are also spread out through the country. All of SaveMart's products are imported from Asia and arrive daily at the San Francisco distribution center.
prompt.question: How would you recommend SaveMart reduce its distribution costs?

clarifying_info.q: How do products flow from the San Francisco DC to the rest of the network?
clarifying_info.a: Every day, trucks transport products from the San Francisco center to each of the primary and secondary distribution centers. Trucks from each of the primary DCs also make daily deliveries to the nearby secondary DCs. Each secondary DC makes one delivery per day to its assigned stores.

clarifying_info.q: Are the delivery routes fixed or do they change with demand?
clarifying_info.a: All routes to and from the DCs are the same each day regardless of demand (static routing).
Trucks are rented and are of uniform size.

clarifying_info.q: Are the distribution centers running at full capacity?
clarifying_info.a: Not all distribution centers (primary or secondary) are at full capacity. The three primary DCs (excluding the West Coast DC) are well under capacity. Most trucks are NOT at full capacity.

clarifying_info.q: Is demand uniform across all stores?
clarifying_info.a: Demand for products is not the same at all stores.

exhibits.title: SaveMart Distribution Center Map
exhibits.shows: A map of the United States showing the locations of SaveMart's primary and secondary distribution centers
exhibits.data: 4 primary DCs (marked as Primary DC): New York, Chicago, Dallas, San Francisco; 20 secondary DCs (marked as Secondary DC) spread across the country

framework: Understand current distribution network structure and cost drivers
Assess capacity utilization across primary and secondary DCs
Analyze truck utilization and fleet economics
Identify consolidation opportunities at DC and truck level
Assess demand variability and its impact on delivery frequency

questions.prompt: What are the main levers SaveMart could use to reduce distribution costs?
questions.guidance: Strong answers structure opportunities across network design, routing, and truck/fleet efficiency. Candidate should identify that static routing and under-utilized assets are key cost drivers given the clarifying information available. No numerical calculations are required for this case.

brainstorming.prompt: What specific actions could SaveMart take to reduce distribution costs?

categories.name: Network / DC Consolidation
ideas: Deliver from West Coast DC only to other primary DCs and secondary DCs on the West Coast; do not deliver from West Coast DC directly to all other secondary DCs
Consolidate secondary DCs that are not at full capacity to reduce fixed overhead

categories.name: Route Optimization
ideas: Determine optimal routes to and from DCs rather than using static daily routes
Switch to dynamic routing: do not make daily deliveries to stores or DCs when demand is low
Allow stores to hold some extra safety inventory so delivery frequency can be reduced

categories.name: Truck / Fleet Optimization
ideas: Consolidate truck loads: combine partially filled trucks to increase utilization
Use smaller trucks on low-demand routes if that decreases total cost
Evaluate buying trucks instead of renting to reduce unit cost if volume justifies it

recommendation: SaveMart should reduce distribution costs through three workstreams: (1) rationalize the DC network by consolidating under-capacity secondary DCs, (2) shift from static to dynamic routing to eliminate unnecessary daily deliveries, and (3) optimize truck utilization by consolidating loads and right-sizing the fleet.
The highest-impact near-term action is moving to demand-driven routing combined with DC consolidation, which directly attacks the root cause of excess fixed-route costs and underutilized capacity.
risks: Other primary DCs may not have enough capacity to absorb additional inventory if the West Coast DC reduces its direct delivery scope
Consolidating secondary DCs magnifies capacity risk if demand increases drastically and the remaining DCs cannot scale quickly
Changing routing patterns may disrupt store replenishment reliability if not carefully managed
next_steps: Determine capacities of all DCs (primary and secondary) to identify which secondary DCs can be consolidated and which primary DCs can absorb more volume
Analyze store-level demand data to quantify variation and design optimal dynamic routing schedules
Review trucking contracts to assess cost implications of changing fleet mix (smaller trucks, owned vs. rented) and to identify savings opportunities
